lesson.title: Triglycerides: The Body's Compact, High-Yield Fuel Tank
lesson.summary: A triglyceride is built from one glycerol backbone joined to three fatty acid tails through three condensation reactions, and this simple three part architecture makes triglycerides the densest, most efficient energy storage molecule available to cells.
lesson.body:
A triglyceride is assembled from two kinds of building blocks you have already met: glycerol, a small three carbon molecule carrying a hydroxyl group on each of its three carbons, and fatty acids, the long hydrocarbon chains capped with a carboxyl group. To build a triglyceride, each of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups undergoes a separate condensation reaction with the carboxyl group of a fatty acid, forming a new type of covalent linkage called an ester bond and releasing one water molecule at each of the three reaction sites. The finished molecule, three fatty acid tails hanging off a compact glycerol backbone, is properly called a triacylglycerol, though triglyceride is the more familiar everyday name for the same structure.

The three fatty acids attached to a single glycerol backbone do not have to be identical, and in most naturally occurring fats and oils they are not; a single triglyceride molecule might carry one saturated fatty acid like palmitic acid alongside two unsaturated ones like oleic and linoleic acid. This mixing explains why a food like olive oil, dominated by unsaturated fatty acids, stays liquid, while a food like butterfat, dominated by saturated fatty acids, stays solid, exactly the packing logic covered in the previous section, just now applied to whole triglyceride molecules rather than free fatty acids.

Triglycerides are the primary long term energy reserve in animals, stored mainly in specialized cells called adipocytes that make up adipose tissue. Compared to glycogen, the branched glucose polymer animals use for shorter term energy storage, triglycerides pack roughly twice the usable energy per gram, both because their carbon atoms are more fully reduced, bonded mostly to hydrogen rather than oxygen, and because triglycerides store in an essentially anhydrous, water free form, whereas glycogen binds a substantial amount of water along with it. That combination makes triglycerides a far more compact way to bank a large energy reserve, which is presumably why animals evolved to rely on stored fat for long duration energy needs while reserving glycogen for rapid, short term glucose release.

Digesting a triglyceride requires undoing exactly the chemistry that built it. Lipase enzymes, secreted mainly by the pancreas into the small intestine, catalyze hydrolysis reactions at each ester bond, adding a water molecule back across the linkage to release free fatty acids and, eventually, glycerol. Because triglycerides are so hydrophobic, the body first has to physically disperse large fat globules into smaller droplets through emulsification, aided by bile salts, before lipase can even access the ester bonds efficiently, since these enzymes work in the watery environment of the intestine and need enough surface area exposed to do their job.

Once absorbed, the fatty acids and glycerol released from dietary triglycerides can be reassembled into new triglycerides for storage, or the fatty acids can be shuttled directly into cellular respiration pathways to generate ATP. Either way, the same simple architecture, one glycerol, three fatty acids, three ester bonds, underlies both the fat stored in an adipocyte and the oil sitting in a kitchen bottle.
